category.title: Sorting Algorithms
category.description: Comparison and non-comparison sorting algorithms and stability analysis.

algorithms.title: Bubble Sort
algorithms.summary: Simple comparison sort that repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in wrong order.
explanation: Iterate through the array N times.
In each pass, compare adjacent elements `arr[j]` and `arr[j+1]`.
If `arr[j] > arr[j+1]`, swap them.
Optimization: Maintain a `swapped` boolean flag. If no swaps occur in a pass, break early (O(N) best case).
After pass `i`, the `i`-th largest element bubbles up to its correct final position at the end.

traceSteps: Pass 1: Compare 5&1 -> swap [1,5,4,2,8]. Compare 5&4 -> swap [1,4,5,2,8]. Compare 5&2 -> swap [1,4,2,5,8]. Compare 5&8 -> no swap.
Pass 2: Compare 1&4 -> no swap. Compare 4&2 -> swap [1,2,4,5,8]. Compare 4&5 -> no swap.
Pass 3: No swaps performed. Swapped flag is False -> Early Exit!

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts an array by repeatedly bubbling larger elements to the right.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Educational purposes, small datasets, or when testing for nearly-sorted array detection.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Computer science pedagogy, simple embedded systems with small memory footprints.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Stable in-place sort with O(N) early-exit best case for already sorted inputs.

algorithms.title: Selection Sort
algorithms.summary: In-place comparison sort that divides array into sorted and unsorted regions, repeatedly selecting the minimum element from the unsorted region.
explanation: Maintain a boundary index `i` separating sorted array `[0...i-1]` from unsorted `[i...N-1]`.
Find index of minimum element `min_idx` in unsorted subarray `[i...N-1]`.
Swap `arr[i]` with `arr[min_idx]`.
Increment `i` and repeat until array is fully sorted.
Note: Makes exactly O(N) swaps, making it useful when write memory cost is high.

traceSteps: i=3: Min in [25,64] is 25 (idx 3). Swap with self.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts array with minimum total element swap/write operations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When memory write operations are extremely expensive (e.g., Flash EEPROM).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Embedded Flash systems, hardware sorting circuits.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Guarantees at most O(N) element swaps.

algorithms.title: Insertion Sort
algorithms.summary: Builds sorted array one item at a time by picking current element and shifting larger elements right to insert it into place.
explanation: Iterate from `i = 1` to `N-1`. Store `key = arr[i]`.
Compare `key` with elements to its left (`arr[j]` for `j = i-1` down to 0).
While `arr[j] > key`, shift `arr[j]` one position right to `arr[j+1]`.
Place `key` at index `j+1`.
Stable, in-place, online (can sort a stream of numbers as they arrive).

traceSteps: i=3 (key=5): Shift 13, 12, 11 right -> insert 5 at start [5, 11, 12, 13, 6].
i=4 (key=6): Shift 13, 12, 11 right -> insert 6 at index 1 [5, 6, 11, 12, 13].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Efficiently sorts small or nearly-sorted arrays and incoming streaming data.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When array length N <= 30 or data is almost sorted.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Subroutine in hybrid algorithms (Timsort, IntroSort), streaming online data.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) best case for nearly sorted inputs with tiny constant factor.

algorithms.title: Merge Sort
algorithms.summary: Classic Divide & Conquer sorting algorithm that recursively splits array into two halves, sorts them, and merges the sorted halves.
explanation: Divide: Find midpoint `mid = (low + high) // 2`.
Conquer: Recursively sort left subarray `[low...mid]` and right subarray `[mid+1...high]`.
Combine: Merge the two sorted subarrays using two pointers into an auxiliary array.
Guaranteed O(N log N) performance regardless of input data distribution.
Stable sort algorithm.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Guarantees worst-case O(N log N) stable sorting.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When stable sorting is required or when sorting linked lists.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Java Collections.sort (for objects), external sorting algorithms, Linked List sorting.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Guaranteed O(N log N) time complexity with stable ordering.

codeTemplates.code:
def merge_sort(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])
    
    res = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            res.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            res.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    res.extend(left[i:])
    res.extend(right[j:])
    return res

algorithms.title: Quick Sort (Lomuto & Hoare Partition)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log N) Average, O(N²) Worst Case
algorithms.summary: High-performance in-place Divide & Conquer sorting algorithm that partitions array around a chosen pivot element.
explanation: Pivot Selection: Pick a pivot element (e.g. last element, random, or median-of-three).
Partitioning: Re-arrange array so elements < pivot are placed on left, and elements > pivot are on right.
Pivot position is now fixed in its correct final sorted place.
Recursively apply Quick Sort to left and right sub-arrays.
Unstable sort algorithm, but fastest in-memory sort in practice due to cache friendliness.

traceSteps: Partition around pivot 70: Elements <= 70 move left [10, 30, 40, 50], elements > 70 move right [80, 90].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts in-place with minimal cache misses and high average speed.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When fast in-place sorting is required and stability is not mandatory.
wAnswers.whereUsed: C qsort(), C++ std::sort (Introsort), OS primitives.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Extremely fast average O(N log N) speed with O(1) extra array memory.

algorithms.title: Heap Sort
algorithms.summary: In-place comparison sort using a Binary Max-Heap data structure to extract the maximum element in logarithmic time.
explanation: Build Max-Heap: Transform array into a Max-Heap in O(N) time using bottom-up `heapify`.
Extract Max: Swap root (`arr[0]`, maximum value) with the last element of the array `arr[i]`.
Reduce heap size by 1.
Heapify Down: Call `heapify(0)` to restore Max-Heap property for remaining array.
Repeat until heap size is 1. Output is sorted in ascending order.

traceSteps: Extract 10: Swap with last [1, 5, 3, 4, 10]. Heapify down -> [5, 4, 3, 1, 10].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Guarantees O(N log N) time complexity with strict O(1) auxiliary space.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When memory is tightly constrained and O(N log N) worst-case time is mandatory.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Embedded systems, Linux kernel memory management, priority sorting.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Combines guaranteed O(N log N) performance with zero extra array memory O(1).

codeTemplates.code:
def heapify(arr, n, i):
    largest = i
    l = 2 * i + 1
    r = 2 * i + 2
    if l < n and arr[l] > arr[largest]: largest = l
    if r < n and arr[r] > arr[largest]: largest = r
    if largest != i:
        arr[i], arr[largest] = arr[largest], arr[i]
        heapify(arr, n, largest)

def heap_sort(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
        heapify(arr, n, i)
    for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        arr[0], arr[i] = arr[i], arr[0]
        heapify(arr, i, 0)
    return arr

algorithms.title: Counting Sort (Non-Comparison Sort)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N + K) where K is key range (max - min + 1)
algorithms.summary: Non-comparison sorting algorithm that operates in O(N + K) time by counting occurrences of keys in range [0...K].
explanation: Find minimum and maximum value in array to determine key range K.
Build Frequency Array `count[x]` storing number of occurrences of each key.
Compute Prefix Sums of `count` array to determine final index positions of elements.
Iterate input array backwards and place elements into output array to preserve stability.
Extremely fast linear O(N) sort when key range K <= N.

traceSteps: Find range: min=1, max=8. Create count array of size 8.
Populate counts: count[1]=1, count[2]=2, count[3]=2, count[4]=1, count[8]=1.
Prefix sums: count[1]=1, count[2]=3, count[3]=5, count[4]=6, count[8]=7.
Build Output: Place elements at prefix sum positions.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts integer values in linear O(N) time without element comparisons.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When elements are integers with small range K (e.g. sorting ages, grades, bytes).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Subroutine in Radix Sort, sorting characters (ASCII 0-255), suffix array building.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Beats comparison lower bound O(N log N) by taking advantage of integer key indexing.

codeTemplates.code:
def counting_sort(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    if not arr: return arr
    min_val, max_val = min(arr), max(arr)
    k = max_val - min_val + 1
    count = [0] * k
    output = [0] * len(arr)
    
    for x in arr:
        count[x - min_val] += 1
        
    for i in range(1, k):
        count[i] += count[i - 1]
        
    for x in reversed(arr):
        output[count[x - min_val] - 1] = x
        count[x - min_val] -= 1
        
    return output

algorithms.title: Radix Sort (Digit-by-Digit Non-Comparison)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(d * (N + K)) where d is number of digits, K is base (10)
algorithms.summary: Non-comparison sorting algorithm that sorts numbers digit-by-digit from Least Significant Digit (LSD) to Most Significant Digit (MSD) using Counting Sort.
explanation: Find maximum element to determine maximum number of digits `d`.
Iterate digit position `exp = 1, 10, 100, ...`.
For each digit position, apply stable Counting Sort based on digit `(arr[i] // exp) % 10`.
Stability is critical: equal digits preserve their relative order from previous pass.
Linear time O(d * N) for integers with fixed number of digits.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts large integers or strings in linear time O(d * N).
wAnswers.whenToUse: When sorting multi-digit integers or fixed-length strings.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Suffix array construction, parallel GPU sorting, card sorter machines.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Outperforms comparison sorting algorithms when number of digits d is small.

codeTemplates.code:
def radix_sort(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    if not arr: return arr
    max_val = max(arr)
    exp = 1
    while max_val // exp > 0:
        count = [0] * 10
        output = [0] * len(arr)
        for x in arr:
            digit = (x // exp) % 10
            count[digit] += 1
        for i in range(1, 10):
            count[i] += count[i - 1]
        for i in reversed(range(len(arr))):
            digit = (arr[i] // exp) % 10
            output[count[digit] - 1] = arr[i]
            count[digit] -= 1
        arr = output
        exp *= 10
    return arr

algorithms.title: Bucket Sort
algorithms.summary: Distribution sort that partitions elements into uniform buckets, sorts each bucket individually (e.g. with Insertion Sort), and concatenates them.
explanation: Create K empty buckets.
Scatter: Put each array element `arr[i]` into bucket index `floor(K * arr[i])`.
Sort: Sort each individual bucket using Insertion Sort or recursion.
Gather: Concatenate all buckets sequentially into output array.
Ideal for uniformly distributed floating-point numbers in range [0, 1).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts uniformly distributed floating point numbers in linear O(N) average time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When input numbers are uniformly distributed over a known interval.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Graphics rendering depth sorting, histogram equalization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Scatter-gather approach achieves O(N) average time complexity.

codeTemplates.code:
def bucket_sort(arr: list[float]) -> list[float]:
    if not arr: return arr
    n = len(arr)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    
    for num in arr:
        bi = int(n * num)
        if bi == n: bi = n - 1
        buckets[bi].append(num)
        
    for i in range(n):
        buckets[i].sort()
        
    res = []
    for b in buckets:
        res.extend(b)
    return res

algorithms.title: Shell Sort (Diminishing Increment)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N^1.3) to O(N²) depending on gap sequence
algorithms.summary: In-place generalization of Insertion Sort that allows exchange of far-apart elements using diminishing gap sequences (e.g. N/2, N/4, ..., 1).
explanation: Initialize gap `h = N // 2`.
Perform h-sorting: Insertion Sort on sub-lists of elements separated by gap `h`.
Reduce gap `h = h // 2`.
Repeat until `h = 1` (final pass is standard Insertion Sort, but on a nearly-sorted array).
Significantly faster than O(N²) Insertion Sort because elements move long distances quickly.

traceSteps: Gap = 1: Final Insertion Sort pass on nearly sorted array [12, 2, 3, 34, 54].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Speeds up Insertion Sort by moving elements across large gaps first.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When fast in-place sorting is needed without recursion stack memory overhead.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Embedded uControllers, uClibc C library `qsort` implementation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Avoids recursive stack space while outperforming simple O(N²) quadratic sorts.

algorithms.title: Cycle Sort (Optimal Memory Writes)
algorithms.summary: In-place unstable sorting algorithm that minimizes the total number of memory writes, theoretical minimum swaps O(N).
explanation: Cycle Sort rotates elements along permutation cycles to place each element into its exact final sorted position.
For each element `item` at `cycle_start`:
Count number of elements smaller than `item` to find its correct position `pos`.
Move `item` to `arr[pos]` and take the displaced element.
Repeat displacement until cycle returns to `cycle_start`.
Guarantees at most N-1 memory writes, optimal for EEPROM / Flash memory lifespan.

traceSteps: Cycle Start 0 (item=1): Already at correct pos 0.
Cycle Start 1 (item=8): Correct pos is 4. Swap 8 into pos 4.
Cycle displacement continues along permutation loop.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts array with minimum possible memory writes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When memory writes cause physical wear (Flash storage, EEPROM) or are computationally expensive.
wAnswers.whereUsed: EEPROM microcontroller memory systems, Flash memory endurance optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Theoretical minimum number of memory write operations O(N).

algorithms.title: Tim Sort (Hybrid Merge & Insertion Sort)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log N) Worst/Avg, O(N) Best (Already Sorted)
algorithms.summary: High-performance hybrid stable sorting algorithm combining Merge Sort and Insertion Sort, standard built-in sort in Python `sorted()` and Java `Arrays.sort()`.
explanation: Partition array into small natural blocks called `runs` (typically MIN_RUN = 32 or 64).
Sort each run using Insertion Sort (which is blazingly fast for small N <= 64).
Merge sorted runs together using an optimized Merge Sort procedure with Galloping mode.
Adapts dynamically to pre-existing order in real-world data to achieve O(N) time on nearly sorted data.

traceSteps: Split array into runs of size MIN_RUN.
Sort runs individually using Insertion Sort.
Merge adjacent runs using Merge Sort.
Adaptive Galloping Mode accelerates merge for long sorted runs.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Delivers real-world peak sorting performance across arbitrary data distributions.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Standard production choice for general-purpose object and primitive sorting.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Python `list.sort()`, Java `Arrays.sort()`, V8 JavaScript engine Chrome/Node.js, Android OS.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Combines O(N) best-case linear speed of Insertion Sort with guaranteed O(N log N) worst-case bound of Merge Sort.
